**On the explanation of "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" (al-basmalah)**

It is related from Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "The basmalah is the crown of the surahs."

It is also related that "a man said in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, 'May Satan be ruined,' and the Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'Do not say that, for he (Satan) swells up because of it. Rather, say: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, for he shrinks until he becomes smaller than a fly.'"

'Ali ibn al-Husayn, may God be pleased with him, said in explaining His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn their backs in aversion﴾ [al-Isra' 17:46]: "Its meaning is: when you say, 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.'"

It is related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "How do you begin the prayer, O Jabir?" He said: "With 'Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.'" He said: "Say: 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.'"

Abu Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Gabriel came to me and taught me the prayer, and he recited: 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful'—he pronounced it aloud."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: These two hadiths imply that it is a verse of the Fatihah. But the sound hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b refutes that, when the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "Would you like not to leave the mosque until you learn a surah the like of which has not been revealed in the Torah, nor in the Gospel, nor in the Furqan?" [p. 59] He said: "So I began to slow my walking, hoping for that." Then he (the Prophet) said to me: "How do you recite when you begin the prayer?" He said: "So I recited: ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ until I reached its end."

And the sound hadith refutes it: "God, may He be exalted, says: 'I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves. The servant says: ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾.'" It is also refuted by the fact that it has not been transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ, nor from Abu Bakr, nor from 'Umar, nor from 'Uthman, may God be pleased with them all, that they recited in their prayers: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful."

It is refuted also by the number of the surah's verses, because the consensus (ijma') is that it has seven verses, except what is related from Husayn al-Ju'fi that it has six verses; but this is an anomalous view (shadhdh) on which no reliance is placed. Likewise, it is related from 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd that he counted ﴿You alone we worship﴾ as a verse, so by his count it has eight verses; this too is anomalous. The words of God, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have given you seven of the oft-repeated﴾ [al-Hijr 15:87] are the decisive resolution of this matter.

Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, counts "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" as a verse of the Fatihah, as do many of the reciters of Makkah and Kufa, though they do not count ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾. Malik, may God have mercy on him, Abu Hanifah, and the majority of jurists and reciters do not count the basmalah as a verse.

What I find more plausible, if the hadiths of Jabir and Abu Hurayrah are sound, is that the Prophet ﷺ saw Jabir's recitation and his relating of the prayer's opening outside the prayer, by way of teaching, so he instructed him to recite the basmalah for this reason, not because it is a verse. Similarly, in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, he saw it as a recitation of instruction. He did not do this with Ubayy because Ubayy's intent was to single out the surah and mark it with the virtue that belongs to it, so he did not add to it what is not part of it. This intent is not present in the hadiths of Jabir and Abu Hurayrah. And God knows best.

Ibn al-Mubarak said: "The basmalah is a verse at the beginning of every surah." This is an anomalous view, and people refuted it.

Al-Sha'bi and al-A'mash related that "the Messenger of God ﷺ used to write 'In Your name, O God,' until he was commanded to write 'In the name of God,' and he wrote it. When ﴿Say: Call upon God or call upon the Most Gracious﴾ [al-Isra' 17:110] was revealed, he wrote: 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious.' When ﴿Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it is: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Naml 27:30] was revealed, he wrote it." 'Amr ibn Shurahbil related that "when Gabriel first came to the Prophet, peace be upon him, he said to him: 'Say: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.'" It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that the first thing Gabriel brought down with was: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." In some routes of the hadith of Khadijah, and her taking the Messenger of God ﷺ to Waraqah, it is related that "Gabriel said to the Prophet, peace be upon them both: 'Say: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.' He said it, and he said: 'Read.' He said: 'I am not a reader'..." and the hadith goes on.

The basmalah has nineteen letters. Some people said: a report reached them that the angels of the Fire, about whom God said: ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:30], their number is arranged according to the letters of "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," one angel for each letter, and they say in all their actions: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," and from there comes their strength, and "by the name of God they were made strong."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is one of the witticisms of tafsir (milah al-tafsir), not of solid knowledge. It is comparable to their saying about Laylat al-Qadr that it is the night of the twenty-seventh, in observance of the word "huwa" (it) in the words of the surah "Indeed We sent it down" (al-Qadr), and comparable to their saying about the number of angels who hastened to record the words of one who says: "Our Lord, and to You be praise, abundant, good, blessed in it," for these amount to some thirty letters. They said: "That is why the Prophet ﷺ said: 'I saw about thirty angels hastening to write it, each wanting to write it first.'"

The letter ba' in "bismi Allah" is, according to the grammarians of Basra, connected to a noun whose implied form is: "an established or fixed beginning, in the name of God." According to the grammarians of Kufa, it is connected to a verb whose implied form is: "I begin with 'in the name of God.'" So "bismi Allah" is in the nominative position according to the Basran school, and in the accusative position according to the Kufan school. Some people stated this without qualification. The apparent view of Sibawayh's school is that the ba' is connected to a noun, as already mentioned, and "bismi Allah" is in the accusative position, connected to something established or fixed, in the same way as "fi al-dar" in your saying: "Zayd is in the house." The ba' of the genitive was vowelled with kasra so that its sound would correspond to its function, or because it only enters upon nouns, so it was specialised in the kind of genitive that occurs only with nouns; and so that it may be distinguished from letters that may also be nouns, such as the kaf in the verse of al-A'sha:

> "Will you desist, while the one who forbids the wayward does not forbid? Like a spear-thrust, in which oil and twisted fiber go."

The alif was omitted from "bismi Allah" in writing, as an abbreviation and for lightness, due to frequent use. The grammarians differed when writing "bi-smi al-Rahman" and "bi-smi al-Qahir": al-Kisa'i and Sa'id al-Akhfash said the alif is omitted. Yahya ibn Ziyad said it is omitted only with "bismi Allah" alone, because its frequent use occurs only there.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God be pleased with him, said: As for other than the name of God, may He be exalted, there is no disagreement on the retention of the alif.

The noun (ism) originally is "simw" with kasra on the sin or "sumuw" with damma on it. According to the Basrans it is derived from al-sumuww (elevation); one says "sama yasmu." On this basis the sin is vowelled with damma in "sumuww." It is also said: "sami yasma," and on this basis it is vowelled with kasra. The waw was dropped from "sumuww," and the sin was given kasra in "sim," as the poet said:

> "In the name of Him whose mark is in every surah, its mark..."

The sin in "bism" was made quiescent by way of irregular (non-analogical) weakening. This original form is inferred from their saying in diminutive "sumayy," in the plural "asma'," and in the plural of the plural "asami." The Kufans said: the origin of ism and ism (both forms) is from al-simah, which is a sign, because the name is a sign of the one it is assigned to; its first radical was dropped by irregular weakening. The diminutive and plural mentioned refute this Kufan view. As for its meaning, it is sound, were it not for what they must accept: that in the diminutive one would say "wusaym," and in the plural "awsam," because the diminutive and plural return things to their roots.

Some exegetes, in this context, raised the question "the name and the named": are they one? Al-Tabari, may God have mercy on him, said: it is not a proper place for this question, and he (Tabari) criticised in his introduction those who speak about this question and its like. But, according to what has been commonly discussed, we say: the noun, such as Zayd, Asad, and Faras, may occur in speech meaning the essence, as in your saying: "Zayd is standing" and "the lion is brave." It may also occur and mean the naming itself, as in your saying: "Asad has three letters." In the first case one says: the name is the named, in the sense that it means the named. In the second, it does not mean the named. From the first usage is your saying: "O Compassionate, forgive me," and the words of God, may He be exalted: ﴿The Most Gracious﴾ [al-Rahman 55:1], ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾ [al-Rahman 55:2]. From the second usage is your saying: "The Most Gracious is a description of God, may He be exalted." As for "ism," which is alif, sin, and mim, it may function in the language of the Arabs in the same way as the essence, one says: "dhat," "nafs," "ism," and "ayn" with the same meaning. On this basis most scholars read the words of God, may He be exalted: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A'la 87:1], and His words: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of majesty and honour﴾ [al-Rahman 55:78], and His words: ﴿You worship not besides Him except names you have named, you and your fathers﴾ [Yusuf 12:40]. They supported this with the verse of Labid:

> "Until the year's end, then peace upon you both; and whoever weeps a full year has made his excuse."

They said: Labid meant the greeting.

"Ism" may also function in the language as the very expression (dhat al-'ibarah), and this is its most common use. Among this is the words of God, may He be exalted: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:31], according to the most well-known interpretations of it. Among this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "God has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one; whoever counts them enters Paradise." In this manner the grammarians used "ism" in the inflection of their terms. What emerges from this is that names may be used to mean the essences of the named things, and in this sense it is said: the name is the named; and names may be used to mean their very expressions, not the named things, and this is what [p. 66] is meant. It has come to me that Malik, may God have mercy on him, was asked about the name: "Is it the named?" He said: "It is not it, nor is it other than it." He means always, in every context, and this agrees with what we have said.

The written form which is pronounced "Allah" is the most awe-inspiring of God's names, and the most frequently used, and it generally precedes all the others; the rest come only as attributes.

People differed about its derivation. A group of scholars said: it is a proper noun (ismun murtajal) with no derivation from a verb; it is simply a name laid down for Him, blessed and exalted, and the definite article "al" is inseparable from it, not for definiteness nor for any other purpose; this is how the name was established. Many scholars held that it is derived from "alaha al-rajulu," when a man worships, and "ta'alaha," when he becomes ascetic. From this is the verse of Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj:

> "By God, the good of the coquettish women, who glorified and sought forgiveness from my bewilderment."

From this also is the words of God, may He be exalted: "wa-yadharaka wa-ilahataka" (and [he] will leave you and your gods) according to this reading, for Ibn 'Abbas and others said: "and your worship." They said: the name Allah is derived from this verb, because He is the one whom every creature worships and adores. This is related by al-Naqqash at the beginning of the surah Al 'Imran. So ilah is fi'al from this root.

It has been disputed: how was ilah modified until it became Allah? It was said: the hamza was dropped by irregular elision, and the alif and lam were added for glorification to "lah." It was said: rather, the alif and lam were added to "ilah," then the vowel of the hamza was transferred to the lam, giving "allah," then the lam was assimilated into the lam. It was said: the original word is "lah," and on that basis the alif and lam were added. The first view is stronger.

It is related from al-Khalil that the original of ilah is "walah," and that the hamza is substituted for a waw, as it is in "ishah" and "wishah," and "isadah" and "wisadah." It was said: the original of the word is "walah," as al-Khalil said, except that it is derived from "walaha al-rajulu," when a man is bewildered, because minds are bewildered regarding the realities of His attributes and thought about knowing Him. The last alif of Allah was dropped so that it would not be confused with the writing of al-Lat. It was said: it was dropped for lightness. It was said: it is a dialectal form which was then used in writing. Among this is the verse of the poet:

> "A torrent came by the command of God, rushing with the rush of a walled garden..."

**(Al-Rahman)** is an intensive attribute (*sifat mubalaghah*, a form expressing intensity) derived from *rahmah* (mercy). Its meaning is that He has reached the utmost degree of mercy, just as *sakran* (intoxicated) and *ghadban* (angry) indicate reaching the extreme of a state. It is an attribute exclusive to Allah and is not applied to human beings. It is more emphatic than *fa'il* (*rahim*), and *fa'il* is more emphatic than *fa'il* of the active form (*raahim*), because *raahim* is said of one who has shown mercy even once, while *rahim* is said of one who does so often. *Al-Rahman* is the utmost extent of mercy. Some people said: *al-Rahman* and *al-Rahim* have one meaning, like *al-nadman* and *al-nadim* (both meaning "companion"). Yes, they come from one verb, but one of them is more emphatic than the other.

As for the exegetes, they expressed *"al-Rahman al-Rahim"* in various phrasings. Among them, al-'Arzami said: its meaning is that He is *al-Rahman* to all His creation in rain, the blessings of the senses, and general blessings, and *al-Rahim* to the believers in guiding them and showing them kindness. Among them also, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Ibn Mas'ud narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "*Al-Rahman* is the Compassionate of this world and the Hereafter, and *al-Rahim* is the Compassionate of the Hereafter."

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: *al-Rahman* is a general name for all kinds of mercy, and it is exclusive to Allah. *Al-Rahim* is only with regard to the believers, as He said: ﴿And He is ever Merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 43]. All these statements are mutually supportive.

'Ata' al-Khurasani said: *al-Rahman* was (a name used alone), but when it was abbreviated and Musaylimah the Liar was named with it, Allah, glorified is He, said to Himself: *"al-Rahman al-Rahim."* So this pairing of the two attributes belongs to no one except Allah the Exalted. This is a weak opinion, because *"Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim"* was before the affair of Musaylimah arose. Furthermore, Musaylimah's naming himself with this was not something established and firmly rooted.

Some people said: the Arabs did not know the word *al-Rahman*, and it was not in their language. They based this on the saying of the Arabs: ﴿And what is al-Rahman? Shall we prostrate to what you command us?﴾ [al-Furqan: 60]. This view is weak. The Arabs only refused to recognize the identity of the God to whom they were commanded to prostrate, not the word itself.

Scholars differed about joining *al-Rahim* to *al-Hamd* (in recitation). It is narrated from Umm Salamah, "from the Prophet (ﷺ), (*al-Rahim*, *al-Hamd*)," with the *mim* pronounced with a sukun, pausing on it and beginning with a cut *alif*. Some of the Kufans recited this way. The majority of people recited *(al-Rahimi al-Hamdu)*, making *(al-Rahimi)* in the genitive case (*yu'rabu* al-Rahimi bi'l-khafd), and the *alif* of *al-Hamd* is connected. Whoever wishes may assume that he pronounced the *mim* with a sukun, then when connecting he moved it for the sake of meeting two consonants, and did not count the connecting *alif*; this is permissible, but the first is more concise. Al-Kisa'i reported from some Arabs that it is recited *(al-Rahima al-Hamdu)* with a fatha on the *mim* and the *alif* connected, as if the *mim* were made sukun and the *alif* cut, then its vowel was transferred to the *mim* and the *alif* deleted. This reading is not transmitted as a recitation from anyone to my knowledge. This is also the view of Yahya ibn Ziyad regarding the Exalted's saying: *(Alif-Lam-Mim. Allah)*.

**Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim**

﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, Musa ibn Ja'far (from his father), 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, Qatadah, Abu al-'Aliyah, and Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hibban said: it is Meccan. What supports this is that in Surat al-Hijr the Exalted says: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾ [al-Hijr: 87], and al-Hijr is Meccan by consensus.

In the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "They are the seven oft-repeated [verses] and the seven long [surahs]," it was revealed after al-Hijr by a short interval. There is no disagreement that the obligation of prayer was in Mecca, and it is not recorded that there was ever a prayer in Islam without ﴿All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. It is narrated from 'Ata' ibn Yasar, Siwadah ibn Ziyad, al-Zuhri Muhammad ibn Muslim, and 'Abdullah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr that the Surah of Praise (al-Hamd) is Medinan.

As for its names: there is no disagreement that it is called *Fatihat al-Kitab* (the Opening of the Book), because its position indicates that. There is disagreement about whether it is called *Umm al-Kitab* (the Mother of the Book). Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan disliked this, saying: *Umm al-Kitab* refers to the lawful and the unlawful. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They are the decisive verses, which are the foundation of the Book, and others that are allegorical﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7]. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: it is called *Umm al-Kitab*. Al-Bukhari said: it was named *Umm al-Kitab* because writing it in the mushaf begins with it, and reciting it in prayer begins with it. Regarding its naming as *Umm al-Kitab* there is a hadith narrated by Abu Hurayrah.

There is disagreement about whether it is called *Umm al-Qur'an* (the Mother of the Qur'an). Ibn Sirin disliked this, but the majority of scholars permitted it. Yahya ibn Ya'mur said: *Umm al-Qura* is Mecca, *Umm Khurasan* is Marw, and *Umm al-Qur'an* is the Surah of Praise. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: its name is *Umm al-Qur'an*. As for *al-Mathani* (the oft-repeated), it was said: it was named so because it is repeated in every rak'ah. It was also said: it was named so because it was singled out for this community and was not revealed to anyone before it, as a treasure for it.

As for the virtue of this surah: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said in the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "Nothing like it has been revealed in the Torah, nor in the Gospel, nor in the Furqan." It is also reported that it is equal to two-thirds of the Qur'an. This equivalence is either in meaning, or it is a preference from Allah the Exalted that is not to be explained by a reason. Similarly comes the equivalence of ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1], the equivalence of ﴿When the earth is shaken﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 1], and others.

Anas ibn Malik narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "*Al-hamdu lillahi Rabbi al-'alamin* has thirty good deeds' superiority over all other speech." Another hadith states that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says: *La ilaha illa Allah* (there is no god but Allah), twenty good deeds are written for him, and whoever says: *Al-hamdu lillahi Rabbi al-'alamin*, thirty good deeds are written for him." This hadith concerns the believer who says it seeking reward, because his saying *al-hamd lillah* contains within it *tawhid*, which is the meaning of *la ilaha illa Allah*. In his saying there is *tawhid* and praise, while in saying *"la ilaha illa Allah"* there is *tawhid* alone. However, if both are taken in their place within the religious law and their role in repelling disbelief and association (with Allah), then *"la ilaha illa Allah"* is more excellent. The decisive evidence for this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best thing I and the prophets before me have said is: *La ilaha illa Allah*."

"Al-ḥamd" (praise) means complete commendation. The alif and lam in it are for comprehensiveness of the genus of praises (istighraq al-jins). It is more general than shukr (gratitude), because shukr is only given for a beautiful act that benefits the one who is grateful, and its being thanked is a kind of ḥamd. Pure ḥamd (al-ḥamd al-mujarrad) is praise by the attributes of the one praised, without his having bestowed anything. So the one who praises among people is of two kinds: the one who gives thanks (al-shākir) and the one who praises by attributes (al-muthnī bil-ṣifāt). Al-Ṭabarī held that shukr and ḥamd have one meaning, but that is not acceptable. It has been related from some people that he said: shukr is praise of God for His favours and bounties, and ḥamd is praise by His attributes.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is a more correct meaning than that they have one meaning. Al-Ṭabarī used as evidence that they have one meaning the correctness of your saying: "al-ḥamdu lillāhi shukran" (All praise is to God, as thanks). In reality this is evidence against what he held, because your saying "shukran" only specified the ḥamd as being for a blessing among the blessings.

The Seven Readers and the majority of people agreed on raising the dāl in "al-ḥamdu lillāh." It is related from Sufyān ibn 'Uyayna and Ru'ba ibn al-'Ajjāj that they read "al-ḥamda lillāh" with a fatḥa on the dāl, and this is by assuming a hidden verb. It is related from al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan and Zayd ibn 'Alī that they read "al-ḥamdi lillāh" with a kasra on the dāl, following the first sound to the second. It is related from Ibn Abī 'Abla that he read "al-ḥamdu lillāh" with a ḍamma on the dāl and the lām, following the second to the first. Al-Ṭabarī said: "al-ḥamdu lillāh" is a praise by which He praised Himself, and within it He commanded His servants to praise Him with it, so it is as if He said: "Say: al-ḥamdu lillāh." On this basis, "qūlū" (say) comes before "iyyāka" (You alone). He said: This is one of the omissions of the Arabs, where the apparent speech indicates what is omitted, as the poet said:

"I know that I will be a grave when the she-camels travel, and it will not travel."

"The questioners said: For whom did you dig?
The informers said to them: A minister."

The meaning is: "The one for whom it was dug is a minister." So he omitted it because the apparent speech points to it, and this is common.

A group read "rabba" with a fatḥa. Some of them said it is in the accusative as a praise (naṣb 'alā al-madḥ), and some said it is in the accusative as a vocative (naṣb 'alā al-nidā'), and on this basis "iyyāka" comes.

"Al-Rabb" in the lexical sense means the one worshipped, the master and owner, the one who manages affairs and sets right what is corrupt in them, and the king. The word comes with these meanings.

From what came with the meaning of "the one worshipped" is the poet's saying:

"Is a lord one over whose head the foxes urinate?
Indeed the one upon whom foxes have urinated has been humiliated."

From what came with the meaning of "the master and owner" is the saying: "rabb al-'abīd wa-al-mamālīk" (lord of the slaves and the owned).

From what came with the meaning of "the one who manages affairs and is their chief" is Labīd's saying:

"And on a day they destroyed the lord of Kinda and his son, and the lord of Ma'add between Khibt and 'Ar'ar."

From what came with the meaning of "king" is al-Nābigha's saying:

"You hasten toward al-Nu'mān until you reach him; ransom to you from a lord, my wealth and my heritage."

From the meaning of "setting right" is their saying: "adīm marbūb," i.e., a set-right hide. The poet said:

"They were like a foolish, stupid she-camel when her milk was injected into a hide that was not set right."

From the meaning of "king" is the saying of Ṣafwān ibn Umayya to his brother on the day of Ḥunayn: "That a man of Quraysh should rule me (la-an yurabbinī rajul min Quraysh) is better for me than that a man of Hawāzin should rule me." And from it is Ibn 'Abbās's saying concerning 'Abd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr and 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwān: "If there must be [a ruler], that a man of my paternal cousins should rule me is more beloved to me than that others should rule me." Al-Bukhārī mentioned it in the tafsir of Surat Barā'a. From that is the poet's saying:

"I was a man to whom my lute was handed over, and before you it [ruled] me, and I was lost, ruled (rubūb)."

These uses may overlap. "Al-Rabb" without qualification, who is the Lord of lords in every respect, is God, exalted is He.

"Al-'ālamīn" is the plural of "'ālam," which is every existing thing other than God, exalted is He. The whole of it is called "'ālam," and its parts among humans, jinn and other than that are each called "'ālam," and in accordance with this it is pluralized as "al-'ālamīn." And since the world of time changes from one time to another, its plural is fitting. The word "'ālam" is a plural with no singular from its own form, and it is derived from "'ilm" (knowledge) and "'alāma" (sign), because it points to its Originator. Thus said al-Zajjāj.
The discussion of "al-Rahman al-Rahim" has already preceded.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 1, verse 4 (part 1 of 2):

The readers differed concerning His saying, exalted is He: (maliki yawmi'd-din / maliki yawmi'd-din). ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read: ﴿Māliki yawmi'd-dīn﴾. Al-Fārisī said: Qatāda and al-Aʿmash also read it thus. Makkī said: al-Zuhrī narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited it thus, with the alif, and likewise Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Muʿādh ibn Jabal, Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr recited it, may Allah be pleased with them all.

The rest of the Seven read (maliku yawmi'd-din), and Abū ʿAmr among them would make the lām quiescent, reading (maliki yawmi'd-din); this is the narration of ʿAbd al-Wārith from him. It is narrated from Nāfiʿ that he prolonged the kasra of the kāf in "maliki", so he read "malakiyy", and this is a dialect of the Arabs, mentioned by al-Mahdawī. Abū Ḥaywa read "malaka" with a fatḥa on the kāf and a kasra on the lām. Ibn al-Samayfaʿ, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, al-Aʿmash, Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān and Abū ʿAbd al-Malik al-Shāmī read "mālika" with a fatḥa on the kāf. These two readings are in the vocative, so that this serves as a preparation for His saying: "Iyyāka" (You alone we worship). Al-Ṭabarī rejected this and said: the meaning of the sūrah is "Say: Al-ḥamdu lillāh (All praise is for Allah)", and upon this "Iyyāka" and "ihdinā" come. He also mentioned that among the eloquent speech of the Arabs is the shift from the third person (ghayba) to the second person (khiṭāb), and vice versa, such as the saying of Abū Kabīr al-Hudhalī:

﻿Yā waylī nafsī kāna jaddata khālidin
wa bayāḍu wajhika lil-turābi al-aʿfari

And as Labīd said:

Qāmat tashkī ilayya al-nafsu mujhishatan
wa qad ḥamaltuka sabʿan baʿda sabʿīnā

(p-76) And like the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Ḥattā idhā kuntum fi'l-fulki wa jarayna bihim﴾ [Yunus: 22]. Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, al-Ḥasan ibn Abī'l-Ḥasan, and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib read: (maleka yawma'd-din), taking it as a past-tense verb. Abū Hurayra read "malīki" with a yāʾ and a kasra on the kāf. Abū ʿAlī said: "None of the readers inclined the alif of 'māliki', and that is permissible, but one does not recite by what is permissible unless there is a widely transmitted report for it."

"Al-mulk" and "al-milk," with a ḍamma or kasra on the mīm, and whatever is derived from them all return to "malaka" in the sense of binding and controlling. Then each derivation of the word is specialized to a kind of meaning. The original sense of "malaka" is shown by the saying of the poet:

Malakat bihā kaffī fa-anharta fatqahā ............................

This describes a stab, and he meant "shaddadtu" (I tightened). From this is the saying of Aws ibn Ḥajar:

Fa-mallaka bi'l-layṭi alladhī taḥta qishrihā ka-ghirqi'i bayḍin kannahu'l-qayḍu min ʿal

He meant "shaddada" (he tightened), and this describes a bow-maker who left of its bark what protects the heart of the bow; "alladhī" is the object, not an adjective of "al-layṭ". From this is the saying of people: "imlāk al-mar'a and imlāk fulān," which is only the binding of marriage, just as they say: "ʿuqdat al-nikāḥ" (the knot of marriage), since marriage is a place of tightening and binding; so the owner of a thing is one who grips it and controls it, and likewise the king.

Those who read "malaka" argued that the word "malaka" is more general than "mālik", since every king is an owner, but not every owner is a king, and the king is the one who manages the owner in his possession so that he does not act except by the management of the king. The exegetes followed one another in citing this argument, but in my view it is not necessary, because they took the two words in absolute terms, not in relation to what is owned and in which the king holds authority. But when the relation of the king is the relation of the owner, then "mālik" is more emphatic. An example of this: let us suppose a great, populous city, and then suppose a man who owns it entirely, or a man who is its king only, managing its affairs and judgments. There is no doubt that the owner has the more comprehensive and greater authority, since to him belongs the implementation of the laws of the Sharīʿa within it, as each person has in his own possession, and in addition he has the power of possessing. Allah's ownership of the Day of Religion is of this degree: He is its owner and its king, and both readings are fine.

Abū ʿAlī related, as an argument for those who read ﴿Māliki yawmi'd-dīn﴾, that the first person to read (malaki yawma'd-din) was Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam, and that a thing may enter into "al-mulk" that does not enter into "al-milk", so one says "mālik of the dinars, the dirhams, the birds and the beasts", and one does not say "malakahā". "Mālik" as a description of Allah, exalted is He, encompasses the king of the essences of things and the king of judgment over them. Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿Quli'llāhumma mālika'l-mulk﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 26].

Abū Bakr said: The reports transmitted refute that the first to read (maliki yawmi'd-din) was Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam; rather, reciting it thus is more widespread. Perhaps the one who said that meant that he was the first to recite it in that era, or that town, or the like.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In al-Tirmidhī it is related that the Prophet (ﷺ), Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, recited (maliki yawmi'd-din) without an alif, and also in it that they recited ﴿Māliki yawmi'd-dīn﴾ with an alif.

Abū Bakr said: The choice in my view is (maliki yawmi'd-din), because "al-milk" and "al-mulk" share one meaning, which is binding and tying, as they say "malakat al-ʿajīn," meaning I kneaded it firmly, and other examples. "Al-mulk" is more majestic and more suited to praise, and the verse was revealed only to extol and praise Allah, glorified is He. So the meaning is that He is the King of kings on that day, with no kingship for anyone else. He said: As for the one who reads "mālik", the way to understand it is to say: the meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, owns that day to bring it about, just as He owns all other days, but He singled it out for mention because of its greatness in its gathering and its events. Abū'l-Ḥasan al-Akhfash said: "One says mulk bayyin al-mulk with a ḍamma on the mīm, and mālik between malk and milk with a fatḥa or kasra on the mīm," and they claimed that the ḍamma on the mīm is a dialect form for this sense. Some Baghdadis related: "Lī fī hādhā'l-wādī milk, malk, and mulk" with one meaning.

Abū ʿAlī said: Abū Bakr ibn al-Sarrāj related, from some of those who chose the reading with "malaka," that Allah, glorified is He, described Himself as the owner of everything by His saying: ﴿Rabbi'l-ʿālamīn﴾, so there is no benefit in the reading of the one who reads "mālik", because it is repetition. Abū ʿAlī said: There is no proof in this, because in the revelation there are things in this form, where the general is mentioned first and then the specific, such as His saying: ﴿Huwa Allāhu'l-khāliqu'l-bāri'u'l-muṣawwir﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 24]. "Al-khāliq" is general, and He mentioned "al-muṣawwir" because of the alert it gives to craftsmanship and the aspects of wisdom. Likewise His saying: ﴿Wa bi'l-ākhirati hum yūqinūn﴾ [al-Baqara: 4] after His saying: ﴿Alladhīna yu'minūna bi'l-ghayb﴾ [al-Baqara: 3]; "al-ghayb" encompasses the Hereafter and other things, but He mentioned it for its greatness, and to alert to the obligation of believing in it, and to refute the disbelievers who deny it. And likewise His saying: ﴿al-Raḥmāni'r-raḥīm﴾, where mention of "al-Raḥmān," which is general, is followed by "al-Raḥīm" to specify the believers with it, in His saying: ﴿Wa kāna bi'l-mu'minīna raḥīmā﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 43].

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
Also, "al-rabb" is used in the speech of the Arabs in the sense of "al-malik", as in the saying: "Wa min qabluta rabbatnī fa-ḍiʿtu rubūbu" (and before this one made me lord, so I was lost, lordships). And other such evidence, so the argument is reversed against those who read ﴿Māliki yawmi'd-dīn﴾.

The genitive in "malik" or "mālik" in both readings is in apposition to the preceding noun in the genitive, and descriptive terms follow the things they describe unless they are cut off from them for blame or praise. The construct with (yawmi'd-din) in both readings is like "yā sāriqa'l-laylati ahla'd-dār" (O thief of the night, people of the house): the noun of time was extended and put in the accusative as an object, and then the construct occurred on this basis. This is not like the construct in His saying: ﴿Wa ʿindahu ʿilmu's-sāʿa﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 85], because "the Hour" is in fact an object, meaning that He knows the Hour and its reality, so its affair is not as the disbelievers suppose in denying it.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
As for the meaning that Ibn al-Sarrāj stated, that the meaning of ﴿Māliki yawmi'd-dīn﴾ is that He owns its coming and its occurrence, the construct with the day is like the construct of the verbal noun with the Hour, because on his view the day is an object in fact, not a noun of time that was extended.

Abū ʿAlī said: Whoever reads ﴿Māliki yawmi'd-dīn﴾, making the active participle construct with the extended noun of time, has omitted the object from the speech, indicating it, its estimate being: "Mālik yawmi'd-dīn al-aḥkām" (owner of the Day of Religion of the judgments). A verse similar to this in omitting the object alongside the time-noun is His saying: ﴿Faman shahida minkumu'sh-shahra falyaṣumh﴾ [al-Baqara: 185], where "al-shahr" is accusative as a time-noun, and the estimate is "faman shahida minkumu'l-miṣra fi'sh-shahr" (whoever of you is present in the town during the month). Had "al-shahr" been an object, fasting would have become obligatory on the traveller, because his witnessing the month is like that of the resident. "Shahida" transitively takes an object; the poet's saying proves this:

Wa yawman shahidnāhu salīman wa ʿāmiran ............................

"Al-dīn" is a word which comes in the speech of the Arabs in several senses, among them "the religion/creed". Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Inna'd-dīna ʿinda'llāhi'l-islām﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 19], along with many other examples of this meaning. And a man's portion of it in his sayings, deeds and beliefs is called "dīn", so one says: "Fulān ḥasanu'd-dīn" (so-and-so is good in religion). From this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying about his dream of the shirt of ʿUmar, which he saw dragging: "It was asked: What did you interpret it as, O Messenger of Allah? He said: The religion." ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: "Love of the scholars is a religion by which one is judged." Among the senses of the word "dīn" is "custom/habit".

From this is the saying of the Arabs about the wind: "Hayf has returned to its customs (adyānihā)."

From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

Kadīnika min Umm al-Ḥuwayrith qablahā ............................

From this is the saying of the poet:

...................................... Ahādhā dīnuhu abadan wa dīnī?

And other examples. One says: "dīn" and "dīna", meaning custom.

Among the senses of the word "dīn" is "the way/conduct of a king and his rule". From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

La-in ḥalalta bi-jawwin fī Banī Asadin fī dīni ʿAmrin wa ḥālat baynanā Fadak

He meant: in the place of obedience to ʿAmr and his conduct. These three senses do not explain His saying: (maliki yawma'd-din).

Among the senses of the word "dīn" is "recompense", and from this is the saying of al-Fand al-Zamānī:

Wa lam yabqa siwā al-ʿudwā / dannāhum kamā dānū

That is: we recompensed them.

From this is the saying of Kaʿb ibn Juʿayl:

Idhā mā ramawnā ramaynāhum / wa dinnāhum mithla mā yuqriḍūnā

From this is the saying of another:

Wa-ʿlam yaqīnan anna mulkaka zā'il / wa-ʿlam bi-anna kamā tadīnu tudānu

This kind of meaning is the one suited to explaining His saying: (maliki yawma'd-din), that is, the Day of Recompense for deeds and the reckoning for them. Thus said Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn Jurayj, Qatāda and others. Abū ʿAlī said: His saying, exalted is He, supports this: ﴿Al-yawma tujzā kullu nafsin bimā kasabat﴾ [Ghāfir: 17], and ﴿Al-yawma tujzawna mā kuntum taʿmalūn﴾ [al-Jāthiya: 28].

The lexicographers related: "dintuhu bi-fiʿlihi daynan" with a fatḥa on the dāl, and "dīnan" with a kasra: I recompensed him. It was said: "al-dīn" as a verbal noun, and "al-dīn" with a kasra as the noun. Mujāhid said: "Maliki yawmi'd-din" means the Day of Reckoning, when they are held accountable and called to account. This, in my view, returns to the sense of recompense.

Among the senses of the word "dīn" is "humiliation/submission", and "madīn" means a slave, and "madīna" means a female servant. From this is the saying of al-Akhṭal:

Rabat wa ribā fī ḥijrihā ibnu madīnatin / tarāhu ʿalā misḥātihi yatarakkalu

That is: the son of a female slave. It was also said: rather he meant "ibn madīnatin" from the cities, the mīm being original, and he attributed him to it, as one says "ibn māʾin" and the like. This verse is describing a vine, and he meant that the people of cities know better the cultivation of the vine than the people of the Arab desert.

Among the senses of the word is "dīn" meaning "politics/governance", and "dayyān" meaning "ruler/governor". From this is the saying of Dhū'l-Iṣbaʿ:

Lāha ibnu ʿammika lā afḍalta fī ḥasabin / yawman wa lā anta dayyānī fa-takhzūnī

Among the senses of the word "dīn" is "condition/state". Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said:

I asked a Bedouin about something, and he said to me: "Had you met me in a condition other than this, I would have informed you."

Among the senses of the word "dīn" is "illness", from al-Liḥyānī, who recited:

Yā dīna qalbika min Salmā wa qad dīnā

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for this piece of evidence (*shahid*), it may be interpreted in a way other than this, so only the saying of al-Liḥyānī remains.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 1, verse 5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You alone do we worship﴾, the utterance of the believer of it is an affirmation of lordship (ruboobiyyah), a display of humility, and a realisation of the worship of Allah, since the rest of mankind worship other than Him, such as idols and other things. The object was placed before the verb for emphasis (ihtimam), and it is the practice of the Arabs to place first what is most important. It is related that a bedouin cursed another, and the one being cursed turned away from him. The one who cursed said to him: "It is you I mean (iyyaka a'ni)." The other replied: "And it is from you that I turn away ('anka u'ridu)." Thus they placed first what was most important. Al-Fadl al-Ruqashi read "ayyaka" with a fatha on the hamza, and this is a well-known dialect (lughah). 'Amr ibn Fa'id read "iyyaka" with a kasra on the hamza and a light (single) ya, because he disliked doubling the ya on account of its heaviness and the kasra being before it; this is like the lightening of "rabbi" and "in". Abu al-Sawwar al-Ghanawi read "hayyaka na'budu, wa-hayyaka nasta'inu" with a ha', and this is a dialect.

The grammarians differed concerning "iyyaka". Al-Khalil said: "Iyya" is a pronoun, to which what follows is added for clarification (lil-bayan), not for definition (lil-ta'rif), and it is related from the Arabs: "When a man reaches sixty, then (beware) of him and of the young ones (fa-iyyahu wa-iyya al-shawabb)." Al-Mubarrad said: "Iyya" is an ambiguous noun (ism mubham), to which something is added for specification (lil-takhsis), not for definition. Ibn Kaysan related from some of the Kufans that "iyyaka" as a whole is a pronoun, and no pronoun is known whose final part changes other than it.

It is related from some of them that he said: the kaf, the ha' and the ya' are the pronoun itself, but they cannot stand alone and are only ever attached; so when they precede the verbs, "iyya" serves as a support (imad) for them, and one says "iyyaka, iyyahu, iyyaya". When they follow, they attach to the verbs and "iyya" is dispensed with. It is related from some of them that "iyya" is an ambiguous noun used to refer to the object, and the kaf and the ha' were added to distinguish between the addressee, the absent party and the speaker, and they have no place in i'rab; so the kaf in this is like the kaf in "a-ra'aytaka Zaydan ma fa'ala".

"Na'budu" means: we establish the law and the commands together with humility and submission. A road that has been made smooth is called mu'abbad, and likewise a camel. Tarafah said:

Thou vyest with swift she-camels that race on, and they follow hoof after hoof upon a smoothed road.

The "iyyaka" is repeated according to the difference of the two verbs, so each of them required emphasis and attention.

"Nasta'inu" means: we seek help from You in all our affairs, and all of this is a disavowal (tabarru') of the idols. Al-A'mash, Ibn Thabbat and al-Nakha'i read "nasti'inu" with a kasra on the nun. This is a dialect of some of the Quraysh regarding the nun, the ta' and the hamza, and they do not say it in the ya' of the absent third person. This applies only to every verb whose doer is named with additional letters, or to what comes from the triliteral form fa'ila yaf'alu (with kasra of the 'ayn in the past and fatha in the present), such as 'alima and shariba; and likewise what has a weak ('illah) middle letter, such as khala yakhalu, for they say: takhalu and akhalu. "Nasta'inu" originally was "nasta'winu": the vowel of the waw was moved to the 'ayn, and it was changed to a ya' because the letter before it was kasra.

The verbal noun is "isti'anah", originally "isti'wan": the vowel of the waw was moved to the 'ayn, then, since the letter before it was opened while it was in the intention of movement, it changed into an alif. It became obligatory to delete one of the two quiescent alifs. It is said that the first was deleted because the second is brought in for a meaning, so it is more deserving of remaining; and it is said that the second was deleted because the first is original, so it is more deserving of remaining. Then the ha' became obligatory as a replacement (iwad) for the deleted letter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 1, verse 6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Guide us﴾ is a supplication (raghba), because it is from the one who is nurtured to the Lord. Thus is every imperative form: when it comes from one above, it is a command.

Al-hidaya (guidance) in the lexicon is al-irshad (direction), but it takes various forms which the exegetes express by words other than irshad, and all of them, when examined, return to irshad.

So al-huda comes with the meaning "the creation of faith in the heart," and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 5], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah invites to the Abode of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [Yunus: 25]. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam﴾ [al-An'am: 125]. Abu al-Ma'ali said: This verse can only be taken to mean the creation of faith in the heart, which is pure guidance.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Huda has also come with the meaning "invitation (du'a)." From that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7], meaning: a caller. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, you invite to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. This too shows the sense of irshad, because it is the beginning of guidance, whether the one invited responds or does not respond.

Huda has also come with the meaning "inspiration (ilham)." From that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He gave each thing its creation, then guided [it]﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50]. The exegetes said: its meaning is that He inspired all animals toward their benefits. This too shows the meaning of irshad.

Huda has also come with the meaning "clarification (bayan)." From that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them﴾ [Fussilat: 17]. The exegetes said: its meaning is: We made clear to them. Abu al-Ma'ali said: its meaning is: We called them. From that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is guidance﴾ [al-Layl: 12], meaning: upon Us is to make clear. In all of this there is the meaning of irshad. Abu al-Ma'ali said: Guidance may also occur with the intended meaning of "directing the believers to the paths of the gardens and the roads that lead to them." From that is His saying, exalted is He, describing those who strive: ﴿He will not allow their deeds to be lost﴾ [Muhammad: 4] ﴿He will guide them and set right their affairs﴾ [Muhammad: 5]. And from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat: 23], meaning: lead them along it.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This very guidance is what is meant in the paths of this world, and it is the opposite of misguidance, and it is the guidance occurring in His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, according to the sound interpretations. This is shown by the word "al-sirat." "Al-huda" is a feminine noun, but al-Lihyani said it is masculine. Ibn Sida said: "al-huda" is one of the names of the day. Ibn Muqbil said:

Until I clearly perceived the guidance, while the deserts were rushing, [the camels] humbling themselves in the mirage, their mouths closed, or they were praying.

"Al-sirat" in the lexicon is the clear road. From that is the saying of Jarir:

Commander of the Believers, upon a path, when the watering places veer, is straight.

And from it is the saying of another:

So he turned away from the clear course of the path.

al-Naqqash related that "al-sirat" means the road in the language of the Romans, and this is very weak.

The readers differed concerning "al-sirat"...

Ibn Kathir and a group of scholars read "al-sirat" with sin (السِراط), and this is the original form of the word. al-Farisi said: it was also transmitted from Ibn Kathir with sad. The rest of the seven, other than Hamza, read with pure sad, and this is the replacement of sin with sad for its harmony with the ta' in emphasis (itbaq), so both are pleasant to the ear; Sibawayh related it as a dialect. Abu 'Ali said: it was transmitted from Abu 'Amr: "the sin and the sad," and "the approximation (mudari'a) between sad and zay," which al-Uryan ibn Abi Sufyan transmitted from him, and al-Asma'i related from Abu 'Amr that he read it with pure zay. Some linguists said: what al-Asma'i related of this reading is an error on his part; he merely heard Abu 'Amr reading with approximation and mistook it for zay, and al-Asma'i was not a grammarian, so he is not to be trusted on this. Abu 'Ali related this statement from Abu Bakr ibn Mujahid. Hamza read between "sad and zay." It was also related from him that he only maintains this in the definite form, not in the indefinite. Ibn Mujahid said: this reading is the burden of a letter between two letters, which is harder on the tongue, and it is not a letter on which speech is built, nor is it one of the letters of the alphabet. I do not deny that it is from the speech of eloquent Arabs, but sad is more eloquent and more widespread.

al-Hasan and al-Dahhak read "ihdina sirataan mustaqiman" without definiteness. Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq read "ihdina sirata al-mustaqim" with idafa. Thabit al-Bunani read "basirna al-sirat."

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning for which "al-sirat" was used metaphorically in this place, and what is intended by it. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "al-sirat al-mustaqim" here is the Qur'an. Jabir said: it is Islam, meaning the hanifiyya, and he said: its breadth is what lies between heaven and earth. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya said: it is the religion of Allah, which nothing other than it is accepted from the servants. Abu al-'Aliya said: it is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his two companions, Abu Bakr and 'Umar. This was related to al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, who said: Abu al-'Aliya spoke truly and gave good counsel.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What gathers from all these sayings is that the supplication is only that the one calling be upon the ways of those upon whom Allah bestowed favour from among the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous, in their creed and in their adherence to the rulings of His law. This is what the Qur'an and Islam require, and it was the state of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his two companions. This supplication is only commanded to believers who already hold the beliefs, and each one has some of the deeds. So the meaning of their saying "ihdina" regarding what is already present with them is: a request for steadfastness and continuance; and regarding what is not present, either due to ignorance of it or negligence in preserving it: a request for direction toward it. I say: every caller who uses it intends the path in its completeness in his sayings, his deeds, and his beliefs, so it is fitting on this basis that he supplicate for the complete path, having some of it already. It is not appropriate that "ihdina" in this verse mean "create faith in our hearts," because that is guidance restricted to a path, nor that it mean "invite us"; the rest of the meanings of guidance are appropriate. "Al-sirat" is in the accusative as the second object. "Al-mustaqim": that which has no crookedness or deviation, and what is meant is that it stands upon the truth and leads to the goal of success and entry into Paradise. Its morphology (i'lal) is that its original form was "mustaqwim," the vowel was moved to the qaf, and the waw became a ya' because the letter before it was kasra.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 1, verse 7 (part 1 of 2):

"Ṣirāṭa alladhīna" is a substitution (badal) for the first "ṣirāṭa." Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and Ibn al-Zubayr read: "ṣirāṭa man an'amta 'alayhim." "Alladhīna" is the plural of "alladhī," whose original form is "laḏḏ," the yāʾ having been dropped for the sake of tanwīn, just as it is dropped from ʿamm and qāḍin. When the definite article "al" was prefixed, the yāʾ was restored. "Alladhī" is an ambiguous, incomplete noun (ism mubham nāqiṣ) that requires a relative clause (ṣila) and a returning pronoun (ʿāʾid). It is indeclinable in its singular and plural forms, but inflected in its dual. Some Arabs inflect its plural, saying in the nominative "al-lazūna." "Alladhī" is written with a single lām in the singular and plural, for lightening, due to its frequent use.

People differed concerning those referred to as the ones upon whom Allah bestowed blessing. Ibn ʿAbbās and most of the exegetes said: he meant the path of the prophets, the truthful (ṣiddīqīn), the martyrs, and the righteous. They derived this from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if they had done what they were instructed, it would have been better for them and stronger in firmness﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 66] ﴿And then We would have given them from Us a great reward﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 67] ﴿And We would have guided them to a straight path﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 68] ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger – those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favor of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous; and excellent are those as companions﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 69].

So the verse implies that these are upon a straight path, and that is what is sought in the verse of praise (āyat al-ḥamd). Ibn ʿAbbās also said: those upon whom blessing was bestowed are the believers. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said: those upon whom blessing was bestowed are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). Makkī and others related from a group of exegetes that those upon whom blessing was bestowed are the believers of the Children of Israel, based on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40]. Ibn ʿAbbās said: those upon whom blessing was bestowed are the companions of Moses before they changed. This and the preceding view are equivalent. Qatādah ibn Diʿāma said: those upon whom blessing was bestowed are the prophets specifically. Makkī related from Abū al-ʿĀliya that he said: those upon whom blessing was bestowed are Muhammad (ﷺ), Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar.

(p-89)The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
What al-Ṭabarī related from him has already passed, that he explained "the straight path" by this. According to what Makkī related, the first view is undermined, and "the straight path" becomes the way of Muhammad (ﷺ), Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both. This is stronger in meaning, because calling the persons themselves a path is permissible.

The readers differed concerning the hāʾ in "ʿalayhim." Ḥamza read "ʿalayhim" with a ḍamma on the hāʾ and a sukūn on the mīm, and likewise "ladayhim" and "ilayhim." The rest read all of them with a kasra on the hāʾ. They differed concerning the mīm. It is related from Nāfiʿ that there was a choice between ḍamma and sukūn; and it is related from him that he did not object to ḍamma on the mīm, which indicates that his recitation was with sukūn. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kathīr would join the mīm with a waw when the hāʾ was preceded by a ḍamma or a kasra, reciting: "ʿalayhimu wa qulūbihimu, wa samʿihimu, wa abṣārihimu." Warsh read the hāʾ with a kasra and the mīm pausal, except when the mīm meets an original alif, in which case a waw is added in pronunciation, as in His saying: ﴿It is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6]. Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, and al-Kisāʾī would use kasra and sukūn on the mīm; when the mīm meets a letter with sukūn they differed. ʿĀṣim, Ibn Kathīr, and Nāfiʿ would proceed with kasra on the hāʾ and ḍamma on the mīm: "ʿalayhimu al-dhilla," and ﴿min dūnihimu imra'atayn﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 23] and what resembles that. Abū ʿAmr would use kasra on both the hāʾ and the mīm, saying "ʿalayhimi al-dhilla" and "ilayhimi ithnayn," and what resembles that. Al-Kisāʾī would use ḍamma on both the hāʾ and the mīm together, "ʿalayhimu al-dhilla," and "min dūnihimu imra'atayn." Abū Bakr Aḥmad ibn Mūsā said: all this difference between kasra and ḍamma on the hāʾ applies only when the hāʾ is preceded by a kasra or a sukūnified yāʾ. When the hāʾ is not preceded by such, the hāʾ takes only ḍamma, and the mīm takes only ḍamma or sukūn, as in His saying: "minkum" and "antum."

(p-90)The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The author of al-Dalāʾil related: some recited "ʿalayhimu" with a waw and two ḍammas; some with two ḍammas dropping the waw; some with two kasras adding the yāʾ; some with two kasras dropping the yāʾ; and some with a kasra on the hāʾ and a ḍamma on the mīm. He said: this is related from the imams and the leaders of the language. Ibn Jinnī said: Aḥmad ibn Mūsā related "ʿalayhimu wa ʿalayhim" with a ḍamma on the mīm without extension to a waw, and "ʿalayhim" with a sukūn on the mīm. Al-Ḥasan and ʿAmr ibn Fāʾid read "ʿalayhimi," and it was read "ʿalayhim" with a kasra on the mīm without extension to a yāʾ. al-Aʿraj read "ʿalayhim" with a kasra on the hāʾ and a ḍamma on the mīm without extension. All these readings have a ḍamma on the hāʾ except the last, and for each one there is a corresponding reading with a kasra on the hāʾ, so ten readings result in total.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿not of those who have evoked anger or of those who are astray﴾. The readers differed concerning the rāʾ in "ghayr." Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read with a kasra on the rāʾ. Ibn Kathīr read "ghayra" with a fatḥa, and a kasra is also related from him.

Abū ʿAlī said: the kasra has two possibilities: as a substitution (badal) for "alladhīna," or as an adjective (ṣifa) for an indefinite noun, as you say: "I passed by a man other than you." It occurs here as an adjective of "alladhīna" because "alladhīna" here is not intended as a specific group; the statement is like your saying: "Indeed I pass by a man like you and honor him." He said: (p-91) The fatḥa on the rāʾ has two possibilities: as a ḥāl, as if you said: "You have bestowed favor upon them, not as those upon whom anger was evoked," or as an exception (istithnāʾ), as if you said: "except those upon whom anger was evoked." The fatḥa is also permissible as "aʿnī" (I mean), and something similar has been related from al-Khalīl.

Among what is cited by one who reads with fatḥa: "ghayr" is indefinite, so it is disliked to describe a definite noun with it. The choice that is free of any doubt is the kasra, and it has also been related from Ibn Kathīr; the preferred of the two readings is the one not departing from the consensus of the readers of the cities. Abū Bakr ibn al-Sarrāj said: "What I hold is that 'ghayr' in this position, together with what is annexed to it, is definite." This is something open to examination and confusion, so let him understand my words: Know that the rule for every noun annexed to a definite noun is that it becomes definite. "Ghayr" and "mithl" become indefinite despite being annexed to definites because of their meanings: when you say "I saw your ghayr," everything other than the addressee is his ghayr; likewise when you say "I saw your mithl," what is like him cannot be counted, due to the many aspects of likeness. They became indefinite only because of the meaning. But when something is definite and has one opposite, and you want to affirm it and negate its opposite, and the hearer knows that, then you describe it with "ghayr" and annex "ghayr" to its opposite, and it is definite, as in your saying: "Upon you is movement, not stillness." Likewise His saying: ﴿not of those who have evoked anger﴾, because the one upon whom favor is bestowed is not punished except by one upon whom anger is evoked, and whoever is not angered upon is the one upon whom favor is bestowed. So whenever "ghayr" has this quality and is intended in this sense, it is definite.)

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
Abū Bakr left "alladhīna" within the limit of definiteness, and permitted describing it with "ghayr" because of what he explained concerning the definiteness of "ghayr" in this position. The opinion of others than Abū Bakr held to the indefiniteness of "ghayr," and went toward bringing "alladhīna" close to indefinite, since it is a common noun not specific to any particular individual; on this basis he permitted describing it with an indefinite.

"Those upon whom anger has been evoked" are the Jews, and "those who are astray" are the Christians. This is what Ibn Masʿūd, (p-92) Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Suddī, and Ibn Zayd said, and ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim related it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is clear from the Book of Allah, because the mention of Allah's anger upon the Jews recurs in it, such as His saying: "and they returned with anger from Allah," and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of what is worse than that as recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah cursed and upon whom He became angry and made of them apes and swine﴾ [al-Māʾida: 60]. These are the Jews, by the indication of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you already know those of you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so We said to them: Be apes, despised﴾ [al-Baqara: 65]. Anger upon them is from Allah, Exalted is He, and the anger of Allah, Exalted is He, is an expression for His manifesting upon them trials, punishments, humiliation, and the like, which indicates that He has removed them far from His mercy, a emphatic and exaggerated distance. As for the Christians, their knowledgeable ones were upon a law before the advent of the law of Muhammad (ﷺ); when it came they went astray. As for their non-knowledgeable ones, their straying has been established since their opinions diverged concerning ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. Allah, Exalted is He, has said concerning them: ﴿And do not follow the desires of a people who had already gone astray and led many astray and strayed from the sound way﴾ [al-Māʾida: 77].

Makkī, may Allah have mercy on him, said by way of relation: "lā" entered in His saying "wa lā al-ḍāllīn" lest it be thought that "al-ḍāllīn" is conjoined to "alladhīna." He said: It was also said that it is emphatic, in the sense of "ghayr." al-Ṭabarī related that "lā" is superfluous, and said: here it is like its use in the words of the rājiz:
"So I do not blame the fair ones that they not mock,"
meaning: that they mock. And in the words of al-Aḥwaṣ:
(p-93) "And it makes me persist in idle play, that I do not love it, while for idle play there is a constant caller, not heedless."
Al-Ṭabarī said: he means "it makes me persist in idle play, that I love it."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The verse of al-Aḥwaṣ means only: the desire that I not love it, so "lā" in it is established in its function.

Al-Ṭabarī said: From it is His saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 12]. "Lā" could be in the sense of omission because a negation preceded it at the beginning of the sentence, so the final clause was made to correspond to the first, as the poet said:
"What pleased the Messenger of Allah was not their deed, nor the two good men, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar."

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb read: "ghayri al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim wa ghayri al-ḍāllīn," and it was related from both of them regarding the rāʾ both fatḥa and kasra in the two words. Al-Ṭabarī said: If someone says: Is not going astray a characteristic of the Jews, just as the Christians have anger upon them? Why then did He single out each group with a separate mention? It is said: They are indeed so, but Allah's marking of each group of His servants with what its expression has repeatedly been used for, and by which He made His command understood.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
This is not a sufficient answer. The matter is that the deeds of the Jews, including their transgression, obstinacy, disbelief, seeing the signs, and killing the prophets, are things that in our custom necessitate anger; so Allah, Exalted is He, named what enveloped them anger. The Christians did not experience anything of this kind; rather they went astray from the outset of their disbelief, without having done anything that necessitates a specific anger over their deeds. Rather, it is what generally encompasses every disbeliever, however diligent he is. Therefore the expression for the two groups was established as mentioned.

(p-94) There is no basis in the expression "those who are astray" for the Qadariyya to claim that they led themselves astray, because this is only like their saying: "the wall collapsed," and "the tree moved," while the one who demolished and the one who moved are other than them. Likewise the Christians: Allah created straying in them, and they went astray through their acquisition (kasb).

Ayyūb al-Sikhtiyānī read "al-ḍaʾḍḥḥīn" with a hamza not extended, as if he fled from the meeting of two sākins; and this is a dialect. Abū Zayd related, saying: I heard ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd reading: "fa-yawmaʾidhin lā yus'alu ʿan dhanbihi insun wa lā jānnun," and I thought he had erred until I heard from the Arabs "daʾbatun" and "shaʾbatun." Abū al-Fatḥ said: upon this dialect is the verse of Kuthayyir:
"... when the spears were reddened with fresh blood."
And the verse of another:
"As for the earth, its dark parts were covered with whiteness, and as for its white parts they were made dark."

(p-95) The people agreed that the number of verses of Sūrat al-Ḥamd is seven: "al-ʿālamīn" is the verse of "al-Raḥīm"; "al-Dīn" is a verse; "nastaʿīn" is a verse; "al-mustaqīm" is a verse; "anʿamta ʿalayhim" is a verse; "wa lā al-ḍāllīn" is a verse.

We have mentioned in the exegesis of "bismillāh al-raḥmān al-raḥīm" the weak disagreement that was transmitted concerning this.

(p-96) The discussion of "Āmīn"

Abu Hurayra and others narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "When the imam says, 'wa-lad-dallin' (﴿and not of those who are astray﴾), then say: Amin, for the angels in the heaven say: Amin. Whoever's saying coincides with the saying of the angels, his previous sins will be forgiven." It is also related that when Jibril (peace be upon him) taught the Prophet (peace be upon him) al-Fatiha (the Opening, the first surah of the Qur'an) at the time it was revealed, and he recited it, he said to him: "Say: Amin." Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Amin" is the seal of the Lord of the worlds, with which He seals the supplication of His believing servant. It is also related that the Prophet (ﷺ) heard a man supplicating and said: "He has made it obligatory, if he seals it." A man said to him: "With what does he seal it, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "With Amin."

The meaning of "Amin" according to most scholars is: "O Allah, answer," or "Respond, O Lord," and similar. This was said by al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and others, and Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab and others explicitly stated it. Some people said: it is one of the names of Allah the Exalted. This is related from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Mujahid, and Hilal ibn Yasaf. It has also been related that "Amin" is the name of a seal with which the books of the people of Paradise are stamped, which are taken with faith.

The implication of these reports is that every supplicant should, at the end of his supplication, say "Amin." Likewise every reciter of al-Hamd (al-Fatiha) outside of prayer, but without loud recitation of the revelation. As for in prayer, some scholars said: every worshipper says it, whether imam, one praying alone, or follower, whether he recites it or hears it. Malik said in al-Mudawwana: the imam does not say "Amin," but those behind him say it quietly, and the one praying alone says it. It has been related from Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) that the imam says it whether silently or aloud. It was also related from him that the imam does not say "Amin" in the loud recitation. Ibn Habib said: he says it. Ibn Bakir said: he has the choice.

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him), says: this disagreement concerns only the imam; there is no disagreement regarding the one praying alone or the follower, except that Ibn Nafi said in the book of Ibn Harith: the follower does not say it unless he hears the imam say "wa-lad-dallin," and if he is at a distance where he cannot hear, he does not say it. Ibn Abdus said: he should estimate the length of the recitation and then say "Amin."

It is a word built on fatha because of the meeting of two sukun letters, and it seems that fatha with the yaa is lighter than the other vowels. Among the Arabs are those who say "Amin" with a lengthened vowel, and from this is the verse of the poet:
"Amin, amin, I will not be content with one until I convey it to two thousand amin."
Among the Arabs are those who say it with a short vowel, and from this is the verse of the poet:
"A great man (fuhtul) moved far from me when I asked him, amin, so Allah increased the distance between us."

People differed over the meaning of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever's saying amin coincides with the amin of the angels." It was said: it refers to answering; it was said: it refers to sincerity of intention; and it was said: it refers to the time. The most preferred view is that the meaning is: whoever coincides in time, together with sincerity of intention and turning towards Allah in longing with a sound heart, and the answer then follows, because whoever is in this state is upon the straight path.
